start-here: Get the foundations right, qualify your prospects, then start small. Use this guide as a practical playbook and adjust to what your own campaigns teach you.
cold-outbound-preflight: Qualify the list, verify authentication, and test actual messages at Google and Microsoft. Check reply, opt-out, and pause automation; exclude warming traffic and keep detailed logs before launching at low volume.
how-to-use-this-guide: Set up domains and mailboxes first, but spend most of your preparation on qualification. Judge server acceptance, inbox placement, and sales outcomes separately.
adjust-as-you-go: Review real replies and grow gradually. When results deteriorate, compare against the last healthy campaign and change one important thing at a time.
provider-requirements-for-cold-outbound: Check the rules for your sending program and recipient providers. Calling an email one-to-one sales does not exempt it from authentication, unsubscribe, or acceptable-use requirements.
mailboxes: Build a credible sender identity around a real reply inbox. Test sending, receipt, replies, bounces, and opt-outs through the actual tool before launching.
spf: Publish one SPF record authorizing the services that actually send for your envelope domain. Avoid unnecessary includes and stay within the ten DNS-lookup limit.
dkim: Publish your provider’s key and enable signing, preferably with 2048-bit keys. Verify the final received message, especially after tools change links or signatures.
dmarc: Confirm that passing SPF or DKIM aligns with the visible From domain. Progress from p=none to quarantine to reject once all legitimate sending routes are proven.
other-records: Make sure MX records allow replies. A real, publicly visible profile photo is more useful for outbound than a BIMI logo; hosted providers generally handle server-level DNS and TLS.
mailboxes-1: Use full inboxes that send and receive at the same address, with no separate Reply-To. Keep one owner per conversation and synchronize opt-outs across every tool.
always-keep-warming: Keep warming active and reserve mailboxes. Use the service’s content identifier to exclude its messages from sales automation and metrics; do not mark them as spam. Check the specific policy if warming itself causes a listing.
for-new-mailboxes: Use the warming service’s gradual ramp. Allow two to three weeks for an urgent launch, ideally a few months; begin real outreach at just 1–2 new prospects daily.
randomization-is-important: Vary warming volume and timing modestly while keeping a gradual ramp. Reduce volume and investigate errors; randomization does not repair a reputation problem.
after-ramping-up: Keep warming with the service’s defaults. As a starting point, use 25–35 warming emails daily, a 30–40% reply setting, and randomized timing; count warming in the overall mailbox workload.
positive-and-negative-actions: Encourage useful replies and make saying no easy. Watch complaints closely, honor opt-outs everywhere, and keep warming responses separate from qualified prospect replies.
personalize-the-messaging: Spend about 80% of your effort qualifying the list. Write early emails manually, then use judgment and the quality of real conversations to decide when AI can scale a relevant plain-text pitch.
randomize-the-body-content: Prefer individually AI-written emails from a proven structure; spintax remains an option. Compare message approaches across similar prospects and senders, and use judgment rather than a fixed reply threshold to scale.
what-not-to-include: Keep the first email plain text, ideally without links, images, or attachments. Remove invented claims, fake familiarity, and anything that distracts from a relevant conversation.
spammy-words: Use specific, defensible claims and normal sentence case. Avoid hype, fake urgency, and excessive punctuation; a word checker is an editing aid, not a deliverability guarantee.
images: Skip images in the first email. Share a useful screenshot later when relevant, and make sure the message still works with images disabled.
links: Ask for a reply instead of adding sales links to the first email. When a link helps, use the sender’s outbound domain and test the final redirect; keep any required unsubscribe mechanism.
attachments: Offer a deck or proposal before sending it. Share expected, safe files after interest, and agree on a meeting before sending a calendar invitation.
keep-markup-similar-to-human-emails: Use plain text, minimal formatting, and a short, accurate signature. Test the actual sent message and keep the reply inbox monitored.
opt-out-and-unsubscribe: Make replying to opt out easy and suppress stop requests across every mailbox and campaign. Include links or one-click unsubscribe where required, and check the rules for each jurisdiction.
subject-line: Use a short, honest description of the business topic. Avoid fake Re: or Fwd: prefixes, and judge subjects by relevant conversations rather than apparent opens.
tracking: Leave open tracking off by default. Optimize for qualified replies and conversations; pixels and clicks can reflect automated activity, and tracking may carry a deliverability or privacy cost.
audience: Spend about 80% of your effort on the right company, buyer, and problem. Exclude suppressed or conflicting contacts, but do not automatically exclude an entire company because one person has engaged.
targeting: Use customer lookalikes and role research to qualify prospects. Keep multiple relevant relationships within a company, coordinate their context, and bring conversations together as the opportunity reaches buying readiness.
buying-intent: Use intent signals to prioritize research, not as proof of interest or permission. Verify the source and relevance, then measure whether these accounts produce better qualified outcomes.
email-verification: Prefer current published addresses and use tools such as Hunter to verify them. Put catch-all and unknown addresses last; revisit them if stronger leads run out or further research supports the exact address.
days-and-timezones: Send in the prospect’s local working hours, with around 9:30 a.m. as a starting point. Default to working days, skipping local weekends and public holidays.
randomization: Spread sends within the recipient’s working window without shortening follow-up spacing. Let the sending provider handle retries and prevent duplicate or catch-up bursts.
metrics: Optimize for positive, qualified replies and meetings held. Exclude warming and automatic responses, define denominators, retain detailed event logs, and review delivery and outcomes by domain, provider, and prospect segment.
google-postmaster-tools-and-provider-fee: Verify domains in Google Postmaster Tools and review available provider feedback. Missing data or zero visible complaints does not prove healthy delivery, especially at low volume.
bounces-deferrals-and-retry-decisions: Save full SMTP diagnostics. Suppress invalid addresses, investigate policy failures separately, and let the sending system retry temporary failures without duplicating queued messages.
spam-traps-blocklists-and-recovery: Pause new outreach and unanswered follow-ups across a troubled domain while continuing real conversations. Fix the cause and follow the specific listing policy; some entries do not clear with rest or continued warming.
a-weekly-sales-deliverability-review: Review delivery, qualified replies, meetings, and contact pressure. Give each issue and interested conversation an owner and next action; check future reminders, message context, and warming exclusions.
interested-replies-and-follow-ups: Aim to answer interested replies within an hour, provide the requested information, and make a call easy to arrange. Follow up contextually if they go quiet, often weekly, and adjust messages as the conversation changes.
postponed-conversations: Use an LLM to extract follow-up timing into structured data, record the future action, and stop generic nudges. One interim update is appropriate only for a major relevant development during a business-related delay, never during leave.
out-of-office-replies: Send no nudges during an absence; resume with a personalized welcome-back message. Contact a relevant named colleague after checking role and duplicate outreach, and accurately say their name appeared in the out-of-office reply.
automating-reply-handling: Start in manual review and automate reliable situations gradually. Keep positive replies more hands-on; routine OOO and negative handling can move to autopilot sooner. Test stop rules, queue behavior, and domain-wide pauses.
testing-inbox-placement: Run placement tests across providers every few weeks and after setup changes. Use the real sending connection, inspect authentication and final message behavior at Google and Microsoft, and compare results with actual prospect outcomes.
message-logs-and-troubleshooting: Keep message and thread IDs, sending context, timestamps, delivery events, authentication results, and workflow decisions. Use this history to investigate missing messages and connect future analytics to what actually happened.
